key_insight: Reinforcement learning for code optimization is much harder than reinforcement learning for code correctness: once execution time becomes the reward, noise, sparse feedback, and training instability can overpower the signal. The paper shows that naive timing-based RL can produce only tiny speedups while also increasing the chance of broken code.
problem_solved: The paper addresses how to reliably use reinforcement learning to optimize generated code for runtime, not just correctness, when execution-time measurements are noisy and rewards are difficult to learn from.
method: Treat code execution time as part of the RL reward, alongside correctness.
Analyze why timing-based rewards are fragile in practice: measurement noise, sparse rewards, and GRPO instability.
Evaluate whether the model can learn to generate faster programs without sacrificing correctness.
impact: This matters because many AI systems can already generate working code, but optimizing that code for speed is a much harder and less reliable problem. Practitioners should be cautious about assuming that reward design for correctness will transfer directly to performance optimization.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: code generation -> execution -> hidden tests -> timing reward -> RL update
Trade-off chart showing correctness vs. speed as reward weight increases
Noise illustration for execution-time measurements with overlapping runtime distributions
Failure-mode icons for sparse reward, unstable training, and broken solutions
paper_authors: Pierre Chambon, Kunhao Zheng, Juliette Decugis, Benoit Sagot, Gabriel Synnaeve
